utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you have a matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a matter as a preliminary matter in conjunction with the Prosecution's request and Your Honours' instructions for us to inquire if there are additional statements that perhaps our investigators or persons working in the field had taken, during proofing last night I uncovered that this witness (redacted) has - I wouldn't call it a statement - but a three-four line summary that he did sign and during the period we uncovered three or so more of those which I bring to the attention only because of the fact that the witness is coming to this court, otherwise I would have got translations and given them all to the Prosecution outside of court. But I have prepared a draft translation of this short, not even half a page, quarter page, what's identified as written statement of the witness who is coming into court this morning; and I've just been able to e-mail that now this morning to Mr. Van Hooydonk, so I hope he's able to pull that up and provide that to Ms. Sartorio, and I apologise for this -- for the manner in which this is done. This obviously came as a surprise to us, but we do want to try to fully comply with the Court's directions and, therefore, went through the diligent efforts to locate these others, and they're all really -- I think once they're translated the parties will see the -- by their nature they're not very detailed. They're more summaries of -- that happen to be signed. They're not really detailed. Fact witness statements as we have come to know the term, but I think they do fall obviously under the ambit of what we do need to disclose to the other party and that is what we're intending to do. So with respect to the other such documents, I have hard copies that I can provide to the Prosecution but I don't know if they want them now or later I can provide them at the break but I did already e-mail the -- the one relating to this first witness MLD18, who is scheduled to be the witness this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, yes. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while I appreciate Mr. Ivetic's candour again this is just one event in a series of -- of events where the Prosecution has not been provided with the material that it's entitled to under the law. We do not have the capacity in this courtroom to instantly print -- print this document. If Mr. Ivetic does have a copy, I appreciate it be given to Ms. Sartorio so that she can be reading it while the witness is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not of the translation. The Defence doesn't have printer here, and the printer's in the Defence room, we're unable to print the document. I could e-mail it perhaps to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy, are you able to -- right. Yes. We'll ask the usher to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to have it printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio just tells me now though that after looking at briefly it appears that it has some material differences from the 65 ter summary, so again, Your Honour, we're here. We're trying to prepare, I mean, we have an important role to play in helping -- assisting the Chamber in ascertaining the truth in this matter; and we're put at a very serious disadvantage when things like this do happen. Your Honour, there's another matter that I would like to raise. Yesterday afternoon, we received the witness list for next week's witnesses. Two of the witnesses on that list are not witnesses that were named on the witness list, filed the 5th of January. While I appreciate the Defence is entitled to submit a motion to amend their list I have not received one as of yet and I am concerned that even if we do, before the close of business today, receive a motion to amend their witness list, it will simply be impossible for us to respond and for the Chamber to reach a decision prior to the time the Defence wants to call these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which is when?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They're schedule for next week. They were notified for next week. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. When are these witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Basically, Your Honour, we will be filing something a little bit midmorning. We stayed up late last night, trying to reorganise the case, and I think this is the sort of reassessment that's going on based on our inability in the field to talk to some of these fragmented witnesses that we'd hoped to call at the request of Mr. Lukic. And that's a tug-of-war that I've had to go through with an attorney with my client as he wants as many people as he knows out in the field to be contacted and brought in. But I, as an attorney, prefer to deal with this from a criminal law perspective in the witnesses we amended were simply an interpreter and one of the main investigators. So as opposed to having to get someone through both of them are investigators actually at some point. But the reality is we think it's more prudent to do some of the cross-examination of the investigative kind of processes that went on in this case to assess the crimes and with people that of course are in the building and on staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. All right, but you're going to file something later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to get it done, Your Honour, but we had it in draft this morning. We've been up since 6.00 this morning it's really hard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Get it to us today. We'll consider it. You know, of course, you have to show good cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We hope to do that. But that's where we're at right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd also want to correct any misapprehension that Mr. Alarid has. One of the investigators, not in the building, he has left the employ of the Office of the Prosecutor. He is currently in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, helping prepare the trial that they are about to start in the coming weeks. I have no idea about his availability. I have not spoken to him since he left here. I also note in the list of exhibits that are intended to be used with him it says and I quote, "All OTP statements in which he has participated in taking," now if that's understood as it's literally written here, Your Honour, Mr. Caine was an investigator for, I think, 7 or 8 years here, worked on the Kosovo case, worked on many cases I only imagine that is dozens upon dozens of statements, many of which may have security issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That obviously would not be granted if --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No and that was [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... for all OTP statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, it was just the ones he touched. There were six of them that he touched in this case, Your Honour, that would be relevant. That's what I meant. I apologise to Mr. Groome for being too broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. We'll respond when we receive the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't any interpretation in English. Would you try again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. As you know, I'm Dan Ivetic, one of the attorneys for Mr. Lukic in these proceedings. Today for the purposes of the record, I will have to address you as MLD18 in order to preserve the protective measures that have been granted by this Trial Chamber. With the -- with the assistance of the court usher, I will now ask to have handed to you a pseudonym sheet; and, sir, when you get this pseudonym sheet, I will ask you to review the same and note if the personal details for yourself, including your name and date of birth, as to the pseudonym MLD18 are accurate. Do you need your glasses, sir, to review the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes. I've left them in my coat pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I can move forward with another question while we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologise I'm just waiting for the transcript. It is coming up. Good. And in what municipality and country do you currently reside and in order to preserve your protective measures, I would ask you to refrain from giving an exact address.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I reside in Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And subject to the same caution about revealing your identity, in which municipality did you reside in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: In Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if we could return to the pseudonym sheet that is before you, if you could examine the same; and if you could please first verify for us that the information contained as to yourself, including your name and your date of birth, is indeed accurate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could look further down on the sheet, do you see that someone else's name that you recognise is listed there with a pseudonym of MLD7 for them? I would ask that if they come up -- if that name comes up during the course of your testimony that you utilise the pseudonym MLD7 rather than the individual's full name. Is that fair and understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes, it's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if you could sign the pseudonym sheet, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, upon signature and submission back to the court usher, would ask that this be tendered into evidence as the next 1D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D102 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, now for the first part of my examination, I would like to go into private session to protect the identity of this witness when going over background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to Mr. Milan Lukic, did you have occasion to -- strike that. On the occasions when you saw Mr. Milan Lukic come to where you were posted, did he come alone or was he in the company of other individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: He sometimes came alone, and sometimes he was accompanied by police officers. I remember once or twice he came with Vidoje Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during those occasions in May of 1992, when Mr. Lukic came to where you were posted, did you have occasion to find out or to -- to see what type of uniform he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Milan Lukic, as far as I remember at the time, was wearing a uniform, camouflage uniform. He probably had a number of different sets. I know that at the time it was camouflage. We ourselves were wearing olive-drab uniforms, and there weren't too many people who were wearing camouflage by this time in late May. Most of the soldiers were wearing olive-drab. And then at a later stage, the remaining soldiers, too, started getting camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is when you saw him coming either alone or with these other peoples, did you have occasion to ascertain with what -- with what organisation in Visegrad he was, at that time, affiliated with, what entity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, I said he came to the post office several times. I remember that. He hung out with Vidoje Andric, the late Vidoje Andric, and some other people who were with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I wasn't really paying attention to that sort of thing at the time, who was hanging out with whom, but as I say, I remember that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You have to be careful that you don't speak when my microphone is on, otherwise your voice will be carried out of the broadcast. That's what I wanted to -- to warn you about that. Now, with respect to your knowledge of Visegrad and the time period when the -- prior to -- prior to the war breaking out and the war breaking out, do you have familiarity with a group known as the White Eagles, and if so, when did that group arrive in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: You see, as I said, all of these things that happened before the war, and as I was telling you, on the eve of the war and before hostilities broke out and the Uzice Corps came in, this Bosniak friend of mine took me to Priboj --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir. Remember we're in open session, so as your giving a -- be careful to not mention locations which could identify your identity. And I apologise. Continue with your answer as to your knowledge of the White Eagles and when they arrived to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: When we returned into town and when the Uzice Corps came, we had this work assignment. We were mobilised in that way for work. We went to work every day, and each day after work, we would go to this cafe, the one that was open. We would assemble there. We would share drinks. We would exchange stories and experiences, who went where, and what, and how, and with whom, and what they did and so on and so forth. And then as I was spending time around town and in that cafe, I saw some people I didn't know who weren't familiar in all sorts of different uniforms with hats, caps; and I heard these people had arrived from Serbia. But the people of Visegrad had called them in and that they were the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to this group call the White Eagles, was, to your knowledge, Milan Lukic ever affiliated with them or commander of such a formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, listen, I told you I met Milan Lukic physically, personally in late May when he started to visit me at the post office. I allowed him to make telephone calls. One thing is sure. I don't remember Milan Lukic hanging out with those people who came in after the Uzice Corps. I remember some people who were spending time in cafes calling out nicknames, and Milan Lukic was certainly not one of them or among them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I want to find out. And with respect to the White Eagles, was it known in the community who the stated commander of that formation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, the talk about town and in the town's cafes was that Dejan Jeftic was in charge, was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to your leaving the White Eagles and returning to Milan Lukic and your encounters with him, did you in the course of your encounters with Mr. Milan Lukic in 1992 have occasion -- strike that. Did you have occasion to have encounters with Mr. Milan Lukic in any years after 1992, and if so, under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I would meet Milan Lukic when he came back from Serbia where he had been in prison. (redacted) So we were neighbours for a while, and we would see each other quite frequently in the pub and also about town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how -- how large is that building where you resided? How many -- how many apartments or floors, if you know? Again without mentioning the exact floor that you're located on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether we should redact the portion of where -- where the -- where the pub was located. I don't know if that number of apartments can lead someone to conclude or narrow down who this individual might be in light of the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you detail for us your knowledge -- first of all, Mr. Lukic had a pub. Could you detail for us how Mr. -- what your -- your encounters with Mr. Lukic in the pub, how was he? How did he react to patrons, et cetera, or interact with patrons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: We knew each other already because we had met when he came to the post office to make those phone calls, and I knew this relative of his. So we new each other, and we would spend some time there together. He would treat us well. He was very fair to us, and he sometimes offered us drinks. He certainly was extremely fair to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about his interactions with other members of the public who were entering the pub?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, he was respectful to everyone. We paid for some of the rounds and some were offered by him. We would just sit there, spend time there, chat away the hours. So that was the setting for the way in which we socialised. This was a town centre pub, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what year or time period was the pub in operation under the auspices of Mr. Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, it could have been late 1993 or perhaps 1994, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Based on your interactions with Mr. Lukic both during 1992 and thereafter, would you consider yourself someone that knew Mr. Lukic well as a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, that's a little vague, but the one thing that I can say is, yes, we knew each other, and I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In all that time that you saw or knew Milan Lukic, did he ever have blonde hair or blue eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Not that I remember. Milan Lukic always had black hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever see him consume alcohol or get drunk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest, in those years of war, there was plenty of soldiers there who drank a lot, and it is perhaps surprising that Milan Lukic never drank, never smoked, and in my presence one thing that I can vouch for is that he never had a single shot of anything or a glass of any sort of alcohol whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. We're waiting for the translation and the transcript to catch up with your testimony. Based upon your personal encounters and knowledge of Mr. Lukic, what would be your appraisal of the type of person Milan Lukic was. And how would you describe him including, if you can, any specific instances you recall that symbolise his interactions with -- with civilians or with children, et cetera, persons of other ethnic groups, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, listen, as far as I'm concerned and our relationship and the way we met, as I said, I allowed Milan Lukic to use the premises of the post office to make telephone calls. We had a good relationship. He was exceptionally fair to me at all times. In 1992, when he was passing through town, I know that the kids loved him. They would run after him, and he gave them candy and chocolate. I know that he was well liked by the town's children. He was their favourite. I'm talking about the time that I actually spent in town myself when I wasn't away on business or another assignment. At those times, I noticed that the kids loved him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can go back into private session, Your Honour. I don't see how I can ask the following questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- without revealing the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I had gotten ahead of myself, forgetting that we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we could again, sir, ask you to detail for us your knowledge of who killed Novica Lukic on around Easter on Mali Vaskrs in 2005.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. If I still recall, it was Mali Vaskrs. That's what we call it, we Orthodox Christians; and we went out. We were in town, and we learned that Novica Lukic had been killed, late Novica, Milan's brother. And it was well known that he had been killed by the Special Police because we could read it in the papers later on. It was publicised. And also, these were the Special Police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and the Special Police of Republika Srpska, at that time point in time, who was the minister of police and from which political party did he hail? I'm sorry, did we get an answer? I'm not seeing anything in the transcript. Sir, do you recall the political party that was in power, at least in the ministry of the police of the Republika Srpska at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall the name. I think that the police chief -- the police chief's name was, if I can remember -- I think that at this time, the ministry was from the SDS; but the minister's name, I can't real little recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect -- with respect to the house where Novica Lukic was killed, had Milan Lukic ever resided there during the time period that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, Milan Lukic resided, lived, in the house above the pub. And I knew the late Novica because he was a co-worker. I used to visit him at his house. When he got married, all -- many of us co-workers went to see them. And also when they had a daughter, we all went to visit him. And I know that Milan Lukic, when he return from Serbia, from the prison, that he lived there in that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what is the approximate distance between the home where Novica Lukic resided and was killed and this apartment of Milan Lukic where he had resided previously? Where Milan Lukic had resided, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, I think about two, two and a half kilometres. In my assessment it's about two and a half kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do -- strike that. And just to back up and clarify one question that I'd missed with respect to the White Eagles, the persons that were in Visegrad known as the White Eagles. Did they -- did those individuals remain in Visegrad the entire duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: When the Army of Republika Srpska was established and after the mobilisation, most of these men left one by one. As far as I can recall, they just sort of dispersed one by one, these small groups of men who were there at the time when the Uzice Corps entered, but I didn't see them after that until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions on direct for this witness, and I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may, I'd like to request that we take the break a little bit early. I had anticipated quite a lengthy cross, but I think that I can shorten it considerably if I have a few moments to reorganise and speak with Mr. Dermot Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Ms. Sartorio; Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Alarid, you have submitted two motions to add witnesses for next week, but when we examine the two, we are unclear as to exactly which witnesses you actually wish to add because there is a sort of overlap and some confusion and not a sufficiently clear identification of the specific witnesses that you wish to add. So at the beginning of the next session, I want you to -- to identify the specific witnesses. Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, MLD18.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: My name is Laurie Sartorio, and I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the nature of his -- of his posting was in private session for purposes of his identification. So I would ask that the counsel be careful in terms of what is said in public session. I apologise for interrupting otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio be mindful of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for that and suppose it will be redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we should go into closed session then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you describe the rest of the uniform that were worn by the White Eagles, what colour, whether you saw any emblems on their uniforms? Can you please tell us as much as you can remember about the White Eagles' uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, they wore all sorts of uniforms. Some were wearing plain clothes, jackets. Some wore hats and some didn't. Some wore camouflage, some not. I mean, different types of uniform. Not all of them were wearing the same type of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know if this group carried a banner, a symbol of their group; and if so, can you describe what the banner may have looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I didn't. I said I saw them there. They stopped by the pub sometimes for a drink. I mean, I say I don't remember them walking about town carrying a banner. For the most part, as I said, I would see them on my way back from work. They stopped by the pub. They weren't familiar, and they weren't from Visegrad. Wearing all sorts of uniforms. They weren't all wearing the same type of clothes or uniform. And people were saying these are the White Eagles that came from some place in Serbia, all sorts of different places. As I said, I didn't see them walk about town carrying a banner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like the witness to be shown a photograph. It is 0644-6597.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, these are the uniforms worn by the White Eagles, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Foundation, calls for speculation. She has to ask first if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- that is really not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness can say whether he knows or doesn't know. Let's not waste time. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These fur hats that they wore, I remember that Jelav [phoen] from Priboj was wearing that -- those White Eagles from Priboj. He was wearing a fur cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it says on the banner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: "With faith in God. Freedom -- freedom," as far as I can tell, "or death." One can't really see very well, but I assume this is an R.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And if we can go up to the -- the face of the man on the right of the photograph with the black hat. If we can zoom in on his hat. Sir, you see an emblem on this black hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not very distinct. I happen to know that the people who were wearing these fur caps wore these coats of arms. I see the outline, and as far as I can tell, there's an eagle on this, and that leads me to conclude that this is an old Nemanjici coat of arms. Two eagle -- two-headed eagle. When I look at the outline, that's how it appears to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And these men in this photograph, these are members of the White Eagles; is that correct? They're wearing the uniforms of the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you know or can you answer that question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said, those White Eagles, those men who were unfamiliar to me, and they weren't from Visegrad, they would come by the cafe, and they were wearing different kinds of clothes or uniforms. Some looked like this, these fur caps, camouflage. Many of them were just wearing plain clothes. Some were wearing this fur cap. Some were wearing hats. They were wearing all sorts of different clothes. They weren't all wearing the same clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this photograph be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like the witness to be shown 0644-6664. This is another photograph. Could you enlarge it just a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, you recognise the man in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes, Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this is the same fur cap that you've been describing that was worn by the White Eagles; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, misstates the evidence. They were shown the one photograph, and he said one of the White Eagles wore a hat like this. And then he said that they were sesirs. Again I return, it's a distinction that has to be made that the transcript reflects.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Furry cap as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, again, the witness mentioned fur cap several times in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And, Your Honour, I'm entitled to make my objection for the record, and I object to the counsel interrupting my objection. I have a right to state my case for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well not when you testify and are coaching the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is she supposed to be talking to me? Is she supposed to be talking to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have a seat. Have a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the fur cap, the fur cap worn by the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see the previous picture that you showed me and this one that I'm looking at now, I mean, fur cap as fur cap, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just attend to the question I've asked you. Attend to the question I've asked you. Listen to the question I'm asking: Do you know the fur cap that is worn by the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, there are different kinds of fur caps. Some people, like, for example, the one that I'm looking at now, to the extent that I could notice the one I noticed a while ago, tapered off towards the top, but this, the insignia, double-headed eagle, this is the ancient coat of arms of the Nemanjic family. On these fur caps this is the sort of thing they wore, the double-headed eagle with a crown. This is an ancient Nemanjic family coat of arms and the subara cap tapers off towards the top, and the flat one is flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is this the same insignia that was on the hat in the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The cap is there. What speculation? It's for him to say whether [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said in the last one he couldn't see the insignia if that is the testimony. He couldn't make out the insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well if he can't make out the insignia, he can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could we enlarge it a little bit further, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Would it be possible to put the previous picture on a side by side since the question was the same as the previous insignia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you want that done, Ms. Sartorio?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can do that on redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We also appear to have a better colour photograph -- a better photo of this in our system, Your Honour, and if I may have a moment to speak with my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've never had a colour one disclosed to us as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's just -- it's exact same picture. It's just a better quality. However, let me just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you recognise what is on this insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, I said didn't I, this is a double-headed eagle with a crown over it. This is the ancient Nemanjic house, Nemanjic family coat of arms; and many people supported this type of insignia, the double-headed eagle with a crown, the old Nemanjic coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you see if there's a skull and cross-bone on this emblem? Strike that. What other -- can you tell us if any other units wore these types of hats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, you see, I know from history that in World War II, I mean the Serbian army, the Chetniks who in World War, I were -- I mean, the Chetniks, that was the name used for the Serbian army from World War I, and they wore these types of insignia, the double-headed eagle with the crown, the old Nemanjic family coat of arms. I mean, I didn't see that myself, obviously, in World War II, but I did some reading, and I know that World War I and World War II, the Serbian army, the Chetniks, wearing this type of insignia, the double-headed eagle with the crown.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what units in the 1992, when the wore broke out in Visegrad, what units were wearing these hats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I mean which unit -- I mean, the army, we soldiers of Republika Srpska, were wearing this, I mean, olive-drab that we had pre-war reservists; and I mean, there was the -- I mean, then the five-pointed star, and when the war began, meaning not everybody had uniforms at the beginning of the war, and then people used all sorts of different uniforms to wear. As I said, this sort of insignia was, as I said, worn by certain Serbs who felt, I mean, greater Serbs than others, to some extent, and they wore these fur caps with this double-headed eagle, this old coat of arms of the Nemanjic family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, this hat was not a part of the uniform of the police officers of Visegrad, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And this hat was not a regular part of the army uniforms of units of the Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, as I said, at the beginning of the war when there were no uniforms to go around, some soldiers from the regular Army of Republika Srpska were wearing stuff like this, while at the other hand at a later time when this, I mean, command of the Army of Republika Srpska had been established and then for the most part, I mean, it was the three-coloured flag of Republika Srpska and later the camouflage uniform started arriving, and many soldiers continued to wear olive-drab for a long time and then later camouflage. But as I said, some of the soldiers, in a manner of speaking, borrowed these fur caps from their grandfathers and grand-grandfathers and there were some regular soldiers being seen wearing things like these. It wasn't [indiscernible] or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that this photograph be admitted -- oh, I'm not finished. Excuse me. Sorry. Could we -- could we focus in on the emblem on the shirt, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to tell us what these words say and what this picture depicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I see the skull, but I really can't read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the phrase "Srpski Cetnicki Pokret." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes. "Serbian Chetnik Movement." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So it says, "Serbian Chetnik Movement." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask that this exhibit be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We would object only as much as a lack of foundation based on the timing of the photograph, otherwise qualified by the fact that, of course, this witness did identify Mr. Milan Lukic as being the person in the photograph. We have no objection for those purposes, but we are somewhat concerned about when the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe there's a sufficient basis for admitting the photograph. The witness has identified the person as Milan Lukic. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, sir, you came here today -- one of the reasons that you came here today was to testify about the good moral character of Milan Lukic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, listen, I'm not here to -- I mean, that's not the reason I came, to speak about the good character and the morality of Milan Lukic. I came here because I was named as a witness, and I was good friends with the late Novica. I knew Milan as well. I am here to tell the truth the way it is. I'm here to tell you about the Milan Lukic that I know. I'm not here to talk about anything else. My friendship with Milan Lukic in all of this period, Milan Lukic has always been very fair to me and my family. I'm not here to discuss morality or character, which are very broad concepts. But one thing that I can tell you is that he always treated me and my family in an extremely fair way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you for answering my questions, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sartorio. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours very briefly. Are we in open session or private session? Open. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the White Eagles, sir, you indicated earlier, it's recorded in the transcript -- strike that. It's recorded in the transcript -- let me just get the exact reference so that there is no confusion. It is recorded in the transcript that you said that when they were in the pub they referred to each other using pseudonyms and code-names. This is at page 33, 2. Is that, in fact, what you said? Did you use the term "code-names" or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I said that they used nicknames. I remember that they called each other Aro [phoen] or Sljivovica. I can't recall them all, all these monikers, but they seldom addressed each other using their first names. They would use nicknames. I remember a man that everyone referred to or called Aro or another one to whom everyone referred as Sljivovica, meaning brandy. Usually they would use nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to these White Eagles that you saw in the pubs, did you ever see Milan Lukic in their company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I said that I saw Milan Lukic for the first time when I met him at the end of May when he came to make a phone call and was introduced by this relative of his. And before that time, I had heard of Milan Lukic but I did not know what he looked like. I didn't know him physically. So we spent a lot of time in the posts office on duty service, but I'm sure that when I met him at the end of May, even if he had been with the White Eagles, once the Uzice Corps entered Visegrad because I did see these men, but I would have known him had I seen him with them. So he was not with them in this time, in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have P229 up on the screen. This is the -- one of the pictures that was shown to the witness by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to clarify the record since the Prosecution did not but left it with their questions making an assertion, the gentleman on the right-hand side of the picture. Hold on one moment. The man on the right-hand side, did you ever see this gentleman with the -- did you ever see this gentleman with the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: I don't know this gentleman at all. I've never seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this hat that this gentleman is wearing, earlier in your testimony, you talked about the White Eagles and the fact that they wore sesirs. Is this --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I mean, can he refer to a particular part of the transcript. I would request if he's referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Gladly. Transcript page 34, line 16 through 19. We have also transcript page 34, 8 through 11. And so I'm going to ask for the -- for that portion to be clarified with the witness since again the Prosecution is attempting through -- is wasn't left -- it wasn't clarified with respect to the questions that the Prosecution asked; so I'm entitled to ask it, and I don't think there's a proper objection to it. I could also ask my questions in B/C/S, in which case the same term would be used, and it would be a proper question and it would not be objectionable to. So really, I think, the Prosecution is making an improper objection in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I didn't mean to make an objection, Your Honour. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The record --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this -- let me restate the question. You -- well with respect to this hat that the gentleman on the right-hand side is wearing, is that a sesir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: No, this is a subara, a fur cap. A hat -- a hat has a brim, but this is a cap that the Serbian folk used to wear in the past. It's a fur cap. As for the people who had come, as I already said, some of them wore a hat, some were bare-headed, but these Whites -- these White Eagles, these were people we didn't know. They came from different parts. And mention was made of some White Eagles who were from somewhere around Priboj, and I know that some of them wore these subaras or these fur caps with insignia, and I think these were the White Eagles from somewhere around Priboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to finish up on that picture, the gentleman on the left-hand side, is he wearing what is referred to in Serbian as a sesir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: This is a Serbian cap called Sajkaca. On the left hand this soldier has a sajkaca on his head whereas the man on the rights has a subara. As for hat --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the army of the Serb Republic what type of headgear or hat did Serbian officers in the army of the Serb republic wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: The officers of the Republika Srpska army wore caps with a blue brim. These were caps with a small --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: -- brim in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say they were caps. What type of cap were they in the Serbian terminology? Was it an sesir, subara, sajkaca or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Neither a hat nor a sajkaca nor a subara but something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to those hats that were part of the official uniform of the Army of Republika Srpska for officers, what emblem was on the front of those hats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: When the war broke out, we all still had these green-drab colour uniforms of the former Yugoslav army with five-pronged stars on them. When the war broke out, most of the people took off these stars off their caps, and they didn't have any insignia. I'm of course referring to those who did wear caps because it was not obligatory to wear them. Later on they would wear a flag, the three-colour flag of the Army of Republika Srpska; so they wore any kind of headgear they could get hold on, whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the flag of the Republika Srpska -- pardon me. With respect to the flag of Serbia, what emblem is on the flag of the Republic of Serbia to this day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Do you mean the flag or the emblem?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me -- let me rephrase it back. What coat of arms is on the flag of the Republic of Serbia's flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I'm not even sure at this point what the coat of arms of the Republic of Serbia is, but I know that the coat of arms of Republika Srpska is the two-headed eagle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is the two-headed eagle the same or similar to the Nemanjic crest that you had referred to earlier? How can you -- how can you compare the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: As far as I know from my history classes, the ancient emblem, the ancient crest, was the two-headed eagle of the ancient Nemanjic State, and it is still referred to as the Nemanjic coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how does that coat of arms of the Nemanjics compare to the official emblem or coat of arms of the Republika Srpska and its organs after -- during that time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: They're rather similar, but I think the difference is in that the coat of arms also has the four S's. Now, whether that is the actual difference between these two coats of arms, the Nemanjici coat of arms and the two-headed eagle crest, some of them did -- one of them does have the four S's and the other doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- want respect to Milan Lukic and the times that you encountered him in 1992 when he came in to where you were posted in uniform, did you ever see him wearing a furry subara hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: No. When he came to make those phone calls, he never had a fur hat on his head. As far as I can recall, he came without any headgear. He was bare-headed and wearing a camouflage uniform. He didn't have anything on his head, no headgear at all, no hats, no subara, no sajkaca. He came without any -- anything on his head, without any insignia on his head. He just came wearing his camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in those occasions when you had occasion to encounter Mr. Milan Lukic coming into where you were posted, did he at any time wear a long beard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MLD18
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, but I'm not certain, but in my recollection he was clean-shaven. He did not have a beard. I don't recall seeing him with a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one last thing with respect to Mr. Tripkovic. Are you familiar with any memorials --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought that they touched on it at the beginning but I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that case, Mr. Witness, I thank you for coming here to testify -- I thank you for coming here to testify. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no further witnesses in The Hague available to testify at this time. I could use this opportunity to clear up the issue with the two filings we had, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should use the opportunity to explain why there are no other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We did not have witnesses who could be here who had visas in time. We had one witness who was schedule for this week whose visa could not be obtained in time. She -- that witness is schedule to be, I believe, the first or second witness next week on Monday. This week was a difficult week to bring witnesses here. Your Honours have heard testimony that was Jovidan [phoen], the slava, this Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. This is the patron saint slava of most of the population of Visegrad, so there were persons that were engaged in activities relating to that slava and, therefore, could not attend to court this week. We have at least two of those individuals -- pardon me, one of those -- two of those individuals coming this coming week. Additionally we have persons who do not have passports for which we have made applications for passports of the Bosnian authorities to try to get those people ready to travel, and there are a certain number of people on our witness list that I have not been able to find, locate, speak with and obtain their voluntary testimony at this Tribunal. So we, as you might recall, this week had had video -- had had some witnesses I thought that were that were anticipated via videolink. Those are now been continued to another time pursuant to the Court's order, so I -- in terms of the number of witnesses that we had planned to try to accommodate this week, we have to take into account that those two witnesses that had been scheduled are not able to proceed this week, and therefore we have this gap of approximately, I don't know, how many witnesses would have fit in this time perhaps one or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dygeus, Philip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you know the matter is not as simple as that. It is not sufficient merely to say that the witnesses don't have visas or you have just applied for passports. The question is whether these things have been done in sufficient time, and I need to investigate it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to satisfy myself before deducting the time from your account. We cannot continue like this. We have a day with three sessions and now we're ending in the middle of the second session. We could easily have done another witness. And if the investigations that I'm going to undertake reveal that there has been negligence on the part of the Defence, then the time will be deducted from the account of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only state for the record again in the past month I've been to the region four times. I sometimes travel twice a week to the region to try to find witnesses and obtain witnesses. This is one of the factors that is the result of the -- the case proceeding in the manner that it has, that we have not been able to have personnel in the field that are able to perform the tasks necessary to bring witnesses here. And I'm not going to go into that in detail because I think we've already done that, and I think I would defer to Mr. Alarid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy please inform the registrar that I'd like a full account of all the information and the requests that were made of them by the Defence in relation to the attendance of the witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know, by illustration, I'd kind of like to just give a point that sort of shows what we've been having to deal with. Like, for instance, one of the witnesses that came this week, the week before to get that passport in order, we had to put a 16-year-old boy on an overnight bus to Visegrad to get it in on time, and a boy goes out and gets a copy and it's as simple as getting that copy; and that copy being essential for what VWS needs to process, you know, this witness. And so it's those kind of -- of unusual steps, I think, that are in a way unprofessional because we don't normally kind of find volunteers to kind of get these things done, but we've been having to resort to do that given our limited resources. So if you want to call it our negligence, I will -- it's not VWS's fault, of course not. They're only able to work with what we give them and in the time-frame we give it to them. But I would say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is whether you give it to them in sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Absolutely, Judge. And I say that we are just constrained by those kinds of problems that I had hoped a different scheduling of this case or different resources appropriated to this case would have been made better for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've always coming back to that, Mr. Alarid, but that issue has been settled. I have been here at the Tribunal long enough to know that Defence counsel are able to get witnesses to court on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is the first case in which I have been involved where there is no -- or there has emerged a pattern of non-attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, have the other cases been a level 1 under the payment scheme that was instituted by the office of legal aid and detention matters, Your Honour. I've been here a long time as well as Your Honour knows; and I can tell you the differences between the cases are very stark in terms of the personnel and the capabilities that are there, I know that speaking as someone who has been a level 3 case and who has had persons full time in the field, something we've not had in this proceeding, and I submit something that makes a great difference as to how we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I must say, Your Honour, we've made this point to the registry on several submissions that you probably wouldn't be privy to, but simply that nothing had been done from an investigative perspective before my, even, involvement as co-counsel. Then all we were trying to do was get alibis done, then trial started, and we've been doing the best we can during trial. That's the -- that's the stark difference, I think as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you are not satisfied with the registrar's decision, you have recourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and that's the difficult thing, Judge, because we're so busy here with you. You know how many filings. You've seen them. You've touched them. As we're trying to prosecute this case, we don't have a division or extra attorneys that can sort of breakdown and do that sort of appeals process nor can we slow you down in order to make those kinds of things happen. And of course then it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who slows down at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Exactly. We haven't slowed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because while the review is being carried out by the President of the Tribunal, incidentally that would not be me, of course, that would be the Vice-President, the trial is proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Exactly. And it's over before we get any response and that's kind of, you know, that's kind of been the pattern and practice. And we just know we've just got to get the job done as best we can, and you're not in a position to stop this trial and give us that time nor is the registrar. I mean, we asked over and over and over again, and if we didn't avail ourselves of the proper appeals process is because, quite frankly, in trial, how do you have the time to do that? Those things should be settled well in advance, and they were not settled nor did Mr. Yatvin, prior counsel, make those appeals because of the lack of communication. I can't -- you know, I just feel that my Defence is taking all the blame for something that -- that was a process that's years older than I am in this case. And I've only been able to do the best I can with the resources that I have and the time I have. And I apologise to the Court for witnesses and holes in the case, but like I said, in good faith we have to talk to these people and get them to you, and with our sources it's -- we've just done what we could, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have a witness for tomorrow -- not for tomorrow, for Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. It's my understanding that I have two witnesses flying in on Sunday according to VWS, so I also have actually two witnesses available for Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The international community which takes a great interest in these trials would be very displeased with what is taking place here. Every other day we are short of witnesses. Did you have something to say -- to clarify the matter that I raised earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we need to go into closed session -- or private session, I apologise, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.00 p.m.,
